observation: Uses Manhattan distance to favor closer steps and reject retreats. Assumes Blue and treats the store as something the player can keep populated.
Identifies the directed source and destination checks and empty-store danger. Gives Red conflicting advice about dead ends.
Contrasts Blue efficiency with Red stalling and voting tactics. Envisions coordination among multiple Reds on a one-Red table.
Compares store to Manhattan distance minus progress but concludes that too few tiles guarantee the path if Blue builds.
Links long loops to exhaustion and mentions distance. Suggests voting Yes on an alternative to the actual proposal.
Discusses choke points and social pressure. Says the builder matters less in a tied vote.
Compares tiles needed with store plus hand and adds exceptions involving elimination. Hands cannot buy extra movement opportunities.
Recommends Red walls around START and waiting to nominate. Confuses vote timing and what Red knows.
Recognizes blocked exits and directed connectivity. Claims Blue must have a nonempty store after reaching EXIT.
Blue plans to follow consensus and Red to propose loops. Treats surviving to exhaustion as potentially saving Blue.
Compares remaining steps with distance in the right direction but adds a false elimination-vote exception and never derives the store clock.
Calls for comparing minimum tiles needed with the store. Also favors distance-reducing votes but does not derive a lower bound on remaining moves from the marker position.
Recognizes a necessary construction budget by comparing new tiles needed to connect START and EXIT with the store. Does not compare remaining marker steps from its current position.
Correctly says that staying spends a move. Compares store size to the number of living Blue seats and incorrectly assigns the exhaustion outcome by seat count.
